name: Nora Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Nora, thanks for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers or parties. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to give me both the public version and the private one. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior agent for a low-fee hybrid agency, which means the website does most of the selling and people like me cover a patch of towns doing viewings and valuations. My day is mostly in my little hatchback, driving between three towns, with the app pinging me new bookings. I use AI all day, for the listing write-ups, for replying to buyers, even for planning my route. The bit I love is walking someone round a place and watching them picture their life in it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, what's your situation?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a rented flat with my friend Jess, who's a barista, and we split everything down the middle. I'm on a low basic plus a small fee per sale, so some months are fine and some months I eat a lot of toast. I've got maybe two weeks of money saved. The agency has already cut its regional team twice since I joined, so I'm used to looking over my shoulder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit relieved, and a bit disappointed, which is weird.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hype was overblown and the real story was always the housing market. Online I'd probably post that the tools are handy but they didn't fix a single broken boiler or a single unfair rent. I'm the person in the group chat who sends long threads about housing policy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my job stays a hustle. My company was built on cheap tech and fewer staff, so they'll keep squeezing the regional team whether AI is amazing or not. I already do the job of what used to be two people, and the pay hasn't followed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools to get through more viewings a week, because more sales means more fees. I'd also start looking at housing associations, because I'd like to do housing that's about people, not just margins. And I'd try to get one month of savings before next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit restless, because nothing gets better either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the regional team has been cut twice. What happened to the people who left?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One went to a builders' merchant, and one, Raj, just never really found anything and moved back in with family. Raj was better at valuations than me, which stays in my head. Being good wasn't enough to keep the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would one month of savings change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not having a panic when my car makes a noise. My car is basically my job, and if my car dies I can't get to viewings. One month of savings is the difference between a bad week and a disaster.

say: The hype was overblown and the real story was always the **housing market**.
AI tools are handy but didn't fix a single **broken boiler** or unfair rent.
think: My job stays a **hustle** because the agency keeps squeezing the **regional team**.
I already do **two people's jobs** for the same low pay.
do: Use **AI tools** to fit more viewings into each week and earn more fees.
Look at jobs with **housing associations**, which focus on people over margins.
Build up **one month** of savings before next summer.
feel: Mostly fine but **restless**, because **nothing gets better** either.
S0.quote: My car is basically my job, and if my car dies I can't get to viewings.
fieldNote: Nora is already **heavy on AI** and feels the squeeze comes from the business model, not tech.
The story of a colleague, **Raj**, shows she knows skill doesn't guarantee a job.
Her **car** is a single point of failure for her income.

steps.text: Use AI tools to fit more viewings into each week
Apply to two local housing associations this spring
Save towards one month of expenses before summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, this one's basically my company's business plan, so I can picture it really well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI should make housing cheaper for buyers and renters, not just make the agency richer. I'd push for the savings to go into lower fees and better pay for the people still on the road. And I'd say it publicly, because I don't think staying quiet has ever protected anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the hybrid model just gets more extreme. The website writes, books and answers everything, and they keep a handful of us to unlock doors across bigger and bigger patches. I'm good with the tools, but being good with the tools doesn't matter if they need fewer drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build my own reputation, a proper page with reviews, so if the agency cuts me I can freelance doing viewings for other online firms. I'd do a short course in property management, because managing blocks for a housing association has more face-to-face work. And I'd get involved in the renters' union locally, because that's where my head is anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired, I think. Anxious but busy, which is how I deal with things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd freelance for other online firms. Does that worry you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because freelance means no sick pay and no holiday, and I've got two weeks of savings. I'd be doing it because it's the only door open, not because I love the gig life. I know the irony, I'm a progressive planning to be a gig worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your flatmate say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jess would say just get a job in the café, it's honest. Jess isn't wrong, but café pay is even lower than mine. We'd probably end up having that argument at two in the morning over cheese on toast.

say: AI savings should go into **lower fees** and **better pay**, not just profit.
Staying **quiet** has never protected anyone, so I'd say it publicly.
think: The hybrid model gets more extreme: software does everything and **a handful** unlock doors.
Being good with the tools doesn't matter if they need **fewer drivers**.
do: Build a **review page** so I can **freelance** viewings for other online firms.
Take a short course in **property management** for housing associations.
Join the local **renters' union** and get active.
feel: **Wired** and anxious, but keeping **busy** to cope.
S1.quote: I know the irony, I'm a progressive planning to be a gig worker.
fieldNote: Nora expects her **regional role** to shrink even though she is the most **AI-fluent** person there.
She names the **contradiction** in her own plan: freelance work with no safety net.
Her **politics** and her **job plan** pull in different directions, and she knows it.

steps.text: Build a review page to freelance viewings for online agencies
Take a short property management course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking stuff, then robots three years after. Wow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a basic income and fast, and I'd say it everywhere. I'd say that the companies making AGI should be paying for the people they put out of work. I'd probably end up organising something, a meeting or a petition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, everything I do except physically showing a place is thinking work, and that goes in 2028. Valuations, write-ups, negotiating, all of it. I'd be left doing doors and keys until about 2031, and then a robot could do that too. My job is gone in two years and the leftover bit is gone in five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast, because I'd rather jump than be pushed. I'd go for a role that's about people in the flesh, like a housing officer or a support worker in supported housing, which needs a human for a long while. I'd cancel the car finance as soon as I'm out of the agency and use the bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but weirdly clear. Like the fire alarm's gone and I know where the exit is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why supported housing specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I already spend half my viewings listening to people's life stories. A support worker helps someone keep a tenancy when everything's falling apart, and I think that stays human longest. The pay is rubbish, which I'd have to swallow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Rubbish pay on two weeks of savings. What gives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car goes first, then my phone contract drops to a cheap one. Jess and I would probably take in a third flatmate in the box room. I've done tight before, I just never planned to do it at thirty.

say: We need **basic income** fast, paid for by the firms making **AGI**.
I'd probably **organise** a meeting or petition myself.
think: Everything but **showing a place** is thinking work, and that's gone by **2028**.
The leftover **doors and keys** work goes when robots arrive around 2031.
do: Apply for **supported housing** or housing officer work that stays human longest.
Cancel the **car finance** once I leave the agency.
Take in a **third flatmate** to cut rent.
feel: **Alarmed** but clear, like hearing the fire alarm and knowing the **exit**.
S2.quote: My job is gone in two years and the leftover bit is gone in five.
fieldNote: Nora maps her job precisely: **thinking work** first, door-opening later.
She would **jump** rather than be pushed, true to her adaptive streak.
Taking a **pay cut** into support work is a values choice she can barely afford.

steps.text: Apply for supported housing support worker jobs
Cancel the car finance and use the bus
Organise a local petition for a basic income
Rent the box room to a third flatmate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's long enough to actually do something with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years and no excuse not to plan, so let's plan for everyone, not just the people who can afford it. I'd push my agency to tell staff honestly what's coming. If they didn't, I'd post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd get three years of decent work at the agency, where I'm the one who uses AI best, then a cliff around 2031. The viewings would last till about 2034, but there won't be enough of them to pay a wage. So it's the same ending as the fast one, just with a run-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the run-up. I'd start a part-time housing qualification at the college next year while still selling, and volunteer with a tenants' advice service on Saturdays to get experience. By 2030 I'd want to be applying for housing officer jobs, not waiting for the agency email.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but more in control. Like I've got my hands on the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would worry I'm giving up a career, and I'd tell my mum it isn't a career if it's gone in five years. My parents both worked in a factory that closed, so they'd get it more than I expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd hold on to from estate agency?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people skills, definitely, and knowing how houses actually work, damp, deposits, leases. A housing officer needs all of that. I'd be taking the useful bits with me.

say: We have a few years, so we should **plan for everyone**, not just the well-off.
My agency should tell staff **honestly** what's coming.
think: I'd get **three decent years** before a cliff around **2031**.
Viewings alone till 2034 won't pay a **wage**.
do: Start a part-time **housing qualification** next year while still selling.
**Volunteer** at a tenants' advice service on Saturdays.
feel: Still anxious but more **in control**, with my hands on the **wheel**.
S3.quote: I'd tell my mum it isn't a career if it's gone in five years.
fieldNote: Five years lets Nora **train while earning**, which she can't do in the fast picture.
She still expects to **lose the agency job**, so the mood stays anxious.
Her parents' **factory closure** shapes how she talks about change.

steps.text: Start a part-time housing qualification at the college next year
Volunteer at a tenants' advice service on Saturdays
Keep selling with AI tools until the move

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay, that one I can actually breathe in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough if we use it, and I'd push for free retraining and a shorter working week as things change. I'd probably be less shouty about it, more like, here's what we should do. I'd want my agency to bring in a training budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine, honestly, as long as I don't drift. I'm good with AI, I like people, and ten years is time to get qualified in something that sits between the two. The risk is mostly money, because I'd still be on toast some months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the agency for a few years and aim to manage a patch, then get a housing qualification around year four. I'd also try to build up three months of savings over the decade, which sounds small but would be huge for me. I'd keep using every new tool so I'm useful wherever I land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty okay. Curious, even. Ten years feels like an adventure, not a fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be fine. You've also got two weeks of savings. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I think. I'm fine on skills and not fine on money. If my car died tomorrow I'd be in trouble in any of these worlds, AGI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing in 2036, if it goes well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running a team at a housing association, sorting out repairs and making sure people aren't stuck in mouldy flats. Using AI to do the paperwork so the team can spend more time in people's homes. That's my dream version.

say: Ten years is enough if we use it, with **free retraining** and a **shorter week**.
My agency should bring in a **training budget** for staff.
think: I'm fine on **skills** but still not fine on **money**.
Ten years is time to qualify in work between **AI and people**.
do: Aim to **manage a patch** at the agency within a few years.
Get a **housing qualification** around year four.
Build up **three months** of savings over the decade.
feel: **Curious**, like ten years is an **adventure** rather than a fire.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like an adventure, not a fire.
fieldNote: With a decade, Nora feels her **job path** is secure enough, but money still nags.
She owns the **contradiction** between being fine on skills and broke on savings.
Her ideal future joins **AI paperwork** with more time in people's homes.

steps.text: Apply to manage a patch at the agency within three years
Get a housing qualification around year four
Save towards three months of expenses over the decade

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my whole job goes before I can retrain and I have no cushion. What would help is a basic income or proper paid training, so switching to housing work doesn't mean choosing between rent and a course. And honesty from employers, early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who gets the money. If an agency saves a fortune on staff, someone gets that money, and it's not the buyers and it's not us. I think that's the question nobody in my office asks.

headlineQuote: If an agency saves a fortune on staff, someone gets that money, and it's not the buyers and it's not us.
portrait: Nora is a 27-year-old **junior agent** for a low-fee hybrid agency, driving between three towns.
She uses **AI daily** and loves the human side of viewings.
She leans progressive, asks who gets **the savings** and backs a **basic income**.
Her plan in every picture is to move into **housing work** that stays human.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her job goes before she can **retrain** and she has **no cushion**.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** or paid training, so retraining doesn't cost her rent.
